extracted.intended_audience: general readers of classic literature; students and readers of Montaigne and moral philosophy
extracted.subtask_short: reading Montaigne: Of Profit and Honesty
extracted.subtask_description: A literary-essay (Montaigne) exploring the moral distinction between profit and honesty, arguing for sincerity, moderation, and the limits of public necessity through historical examples and anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the honest over the profitable
rubrics_metrics.description: One should abandon profitable measures when they are dishonest; prefer honour and uprightness even when profit is available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Tiberius refusing a treacherous assassination of Arminius: 'he quitted the profitable for the honest.' Montaigne holds that honourable restraint is a virtue even if it sacrifices political or material advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and plain speaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity and pure truth are valuable and disarming; speaking openly without dissembling is preferable to cunning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne claims an open, blunt manner 'passes for current' and clears one from suspicion; he contrasts candid speech with the craft of negotiators and praises simple frankness as a reliable social currency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not be swayed by passion in public duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid letting love, hatred, or private passions dictate actions concerning public affairs or judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimate intentions should be temperate and equable; passions are useful only to those who cannot make use of reason. Examples include retaining moderation toward princes and public causes without being captive to private interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public duty may require harsh acts but must be circumscribed
rubrics_metrics.description: When a public necessity truly demands it, a ruler may be forced to override ordinary duty, but such cases are rare, painful, and should be undertaken with regret and restraint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne allows that a prince constrained by extreme necessity can break private faith for public preservation, but insists this is misfortune, not vice, and should weigh heavily on conscience. Use Timoleon as example of subsequent atonement and public judgment being divided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treachery is only potentially excusable to punish treachery
rubrics_metrics.description: Treachery can at most be excused when it is practised in order to chastise or counteract another treachery; otherwise it is condemnable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne cites historical punishments of traitors (e.g., those who betray for reward later executed) to show that even successful treachery is often deemed execrable; the only slender justification is a retaliatory chastisement of treachery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice should avoid malicious deceit
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial or official procedures that use cozenage, false hopes, or deceit to elicit confessions are malicious and stain justice itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticizes judges who allure criminals by false promises; he finds it 'a malicious kind of justice' and prefers alternatives that do not rely on treacherous means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refuse to accept commissions requiring lying or betrayal
rubrics_metrics.description: A person of honour should not accept employment or commissions whose performance would require lying, betraying, or perjury, even if demanded for public service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne asserts he would rather be punished than serve in offices that demand deceit; he recounts oath-exempt judges and Lacedaemonian stance: taxes may be imposed but not commands to commit dishonour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep promises and oaths except when the promise is inherently wicked
rubrics_metrics.description: Promises made under fear are still obligations; one should honour them unless the promise itself required one to commit something unlawful or wicked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues against the philosophical claim that an oath to robbers is void once free: fear-induced words bind; only intrinsically unlawful promises justify breach. Montaigne reports he disowns careless words but otherwise keeps his word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in political engagement and selection of service
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not overcommit to public employments or partisan extremes; choose limited, honest service rather than full subjection that makes a freeman into a slave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne prefers private life or restrained, principled participation in public affairs; he warns against those who expect unconditional obedience from freemen and praises those who accept limited trusts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid double-dealing and maintain loyalty within role boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Serving both sides or double-dealing is morally and prudentially bad: it brands one untrustworthy and can be exploited by both parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne condemns offering full service to rival parties; a double-dealer will be considered a villain and used for intelligence, then discarded. He limits himself to neutral or known statements to both sides when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the distinction between natural/true justice and special/national justice
rubrics_metrics.description: True, universal justice differs from the ad hoc, national justice of governments, which often permits or introduces vicious actions for state ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne cites Cicero: we retain only a shadow of true justice; senates and laws may enact or permit crimes. This alerts readers to moral skepticism about official justifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that some useful vices exist, but judge them carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: There are vices (and actions) that are lawful or useful for public ends; recognizing their utility does not erase their moral stain and demands prudence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne admits that deceit and other vices 'maintain and supply most men's employment' and that some public offices require ignoble acts; nonetheless, he treats these as morally costly and not to be undertaken lightly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit acceptance of secrets and burdensome trusts
rubrics_metrics.description: One should accept as few secrets and burdensome confidences as possible because secrecy is a troublesome burden and invites corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne prefers to know only what he must for his function and avoid deeper intrusions; he claims that secrets of princes are a troublesome burden and recounts Philippides' witty reply about accepting no secrets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act with authenticity rather than calculated affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural simplicity and apparent liberty of manner are preferable to counterfeit subtleties and affected prudence; authenticity should match the role that suits one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne defends his plainness against critics who call it artful subtlety, arguing his natural behaviour is consistent through varied situations and not an affected mask. Be wary of people who mimic roles ill-suited to them (Aesop's ass anecdote).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary public acts require personal atonement or public absolution
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person commits morally dubious acts for the public good, they should expect divided judgment and the need to justify or atone personally; public expedients do not erase moral responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Timoleon, who killed his brother but then shed tears and was judged ambiguously by the Senate and citizens; Montaigne emphasizes the need for remorse and the narrowness of such excuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of official compensations that mask crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who profit by vicious public acts often attempt to cloak them with a show of virtue or punishment of perpetrators to erase memory of the deed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne observes rulers who punish their instruments after the fact (e.g., hanged servants with reward pouches, or rulers punishing those who carried out their crimes) as a way to wipe responsibility and present a veneer of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: The limits of conscience: some will choose death over committing immoral acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal conscience may make it more honorable to die than to commit certain acts demanded by authority; such refusal can be morally praiseworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne praises those who would rather be thought guilty than serve by committing parricide or other shameful executions (Amurath I example) and those who chose not to hang companions to save themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate public examples skeptically when used to justify immoral means
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept philosophical examples or casuistry that too readily justify breaking faith or promises under pretexts; examine the true weight of circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne disputes some philosophical rules used to prefer public utility over faith (e.g., the robber/oath case), insisting such examples often lack necessary circumstantial weight to absolve moral breach.
